stem: Evaluate the impacts of anti-natalist and pro-natalist policies on birth rates. Refer to named countries.

points.description: Anti-natalist example (e.g. China): measures described (one child; bonuses and fines).
Impact: fertility fell sharply / slower growth.
Other factors also lowered births (economic growth, urbanisation, education) so not all due to policy.
Side effects: gender imbalance, ageing, 4-2-1, human-rights concerns.
Pro-natalist example (e.g. France or Singapore): allowances, tax cuts, childcare, leave.
Impact: France relatively high fertility for Europe but below replacement; Singapore still very low; expensive.
Judgement: easier to lower than raise births; voluntary policies with education are fairer.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: China's one-child policy, introduced in about 1979-1980, rewarded couples with one child and fined those with more. Fertility fell sharply and growth slowed, although rapid economic growth and urbanisation would also have lowered births. The policy caused a gender imbalance, an ageing population and human-rights concerns, and even after it was relaxed to two children in 2016 and three in 2021 births stayed low. France's pro-natalist policy of allowances, tax reductions and subsidised childcare has kept fertility among the highest in the EU, but still below replacement, and it is costly. Singapore changed from 'Stop at Two' to encouraging births, yet fertility remains very low. Overall, anti-natalist policies can lower birth rates strongly, but pro-natalist policies have only modest effects, suggesting that it is easier to reduce births than to raise them.

explanation: Two policy types, evidence and a judgement.
hints: Use one anti-natalist and one pro-natalist example; judge the effect on birth rates.
